title: Repository Guidelines
text:
The Quarto project lives at the repository root. _quarto.yml drives navigation and global settings. Content sources stay grouped by theme: internship/ for report sections, reflections/week-01|week-02/ for daily logs, plus learning-outcomes/, coursework/, and artefacts/. Assets reside in images/, while custom styling belongs in styles/custom.css. Generated HTML is emitted to _site/; do not edit files there directly because each render overwrites them.



Run commands from the repository root. quarto preview launches a hot-reloading dev server; add --port 4242 if the default port conflicts. quarto render performs a clean production build into _site/. Use quarto publish gh-pages to push the rendered site to GitHub Pages once the build passes locally. When debugging, quarto check validates dependencies and project metadata.



Author narrative content in Quarto Markdown with meaningful headings and limited line wrapping. Keep YAML front matter indented with two spaces to match _quarto.yml. Follow existing slug patterns such as day-01.qmd for reflections and index.qmd for landing pages. Store images as lowercase, hyphenated filenames in images/, and reference them with relative paths. Extend styling in styles/custom.css, using descriptive class names and concise comments for nontrivial rules.



Before opening a pull request, run quarto render and review the console for warnings. Manually inspect key pages in the rendered _site/, ensuring navigation links, cross-references, and downloads resolve. For navigation or configuration edits, run quarto check to confirm metadata consistency. Use the README quality checklist to verify reflections, artefacts, and assets stay complete.



History favours concise summary lines such as Remove large PDFs from repo; keep commits scoped to a single theme and use sentence case in 50 characters or fewer. Reference related reflections or artefacts in the body when context is helpful. Pull requests should describe the change, note outstanding TODOs, and include screenshots or preview URLs when layout shifts. Link coursework milestones or issues so reviewers can trace academic requirements.



Archive supporting documents in artefacts/ and cite them from the relevant reflection. Optimise images before adding them to images/ to keep the repository lightweight. For internship updates, refresh internship/index.qmd first so navigation highlights the latest summary, then cascade changes to companion pages.

title: Introduction & Background
text:
I am a final year master’s student at Stellenbosch University, in the final stages of my MSc in Biostatistics. My degree began with a year focused on both foundational and advanced coursework, which aimed to equip students with statistical methods relevant to biostatistics. These theoretical modules were assessed by lecturers using both formative and summative methods.
After completing the foundational coursework in my first year, I progressed to my second year, where I enrolled in the Biostatistical Consulting (BC) module. The BC module was designed by experienced biostatisticians to merge theoretical concepts with practical implementation, placing particular importance on developing collaborative abilities through interactive lectures and experiential learning opportunities. Unlike the more conventional, lecture-based modules, the BC module placed a strong emphasis on discussion, questioning, and the development of practical collaboration skills essential for effective biostatistical consulting.
Following the completion of this module, I began my internship at Scigenix Pty (Ltd) on 23 June 2025, which concluded on 30 September 2025. This three-month placement offered me the opportunity to apply not only the skills fostered in the BC module but also those learned throughout my MSc. Through this internship, I honed my ability to communicate complex statistical concepts to non-specialist audiences, which is a skill I now regard as essential for successful collaboration in clinical research.

title: Introduction & Background
text:
Background of Organisation
Scigenix is a dynamic clinical research organisation that specializes in data-driven solutions for the pharmaceutical and healthcare sectors, with a particular focus on clinical trials. With a global team of experts, the company brings together a wide range of skills, including data science, biostatistics, data management, and medical writing. Its strength lies in leveraging open-source technologies, like programming in R as opossed to SAS, to deliver cost-effective, precise, and scalable solutions across the full spectrum of clinical research. Be it from the initial study design to the final steps of regulatory submission, which is the formal process of submitting research findings to health authorities for review and approval.
The organization positions itself as a change-maker in the clinical research world, particularly in addressing challenges related to data collection, cleaning, analysis, and reporting under strict regulatory constraints. These constraints are guidelines and requirements set up by authorities, like the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), to regulate the conduct of clinical trials. If not addressed effectively, such challenges can lead to delayed drug approvals and substantial financial losses for sponsors. Scigenix fills this gap by offering streamlined, AI-supported data processing and analysis pipelines that support faster, higher-quality decision-making along with a fantastic team of biostatisticians who I have the pleasure working alongside of.
Beyond technical capabilities, Scigenix is defined by its strong internal culture and values. These include scientific excellence, attention to detail, client-centricity, a collaborative spirit, and a supportive work environment. A fair bit of humour also makes the workplace an enjoyable and engaging environment in what is often seen as a dull and dreery industry
In the biostatistics unit where I was placed, R is the primary programming language used for analysis and reporting. Each project is structured as a self-contained software solution, often in the form of an R package. An R package is a collection of code and documentation that standardizes analysis workflows, ensuring consistency and reproducibility in research findings. This approach allows for transparency and good software development practices. The biostatistics unit supports all phases of clinical research, with a particular emphasis on robust statistical methodologies, clear documentation, and regulatory compliance. I observed an exponential improvement in my own programming abilities over the course of my internship as I was exposed to best practices in R programming, version control using Git, and collaborative development workflows.
Scigenix’s long-term vision is to become a transformative force in the clinical research industry, especially as an advocate for open-source solutions, while keeping its commitment to quality, accessibility, and innovation.

title: Introduction & Background
text:
Life at Scigenix
The Scigenix office is based in a converted home in Hazelwood, Pretoria—a residential area that has, in recent years, transformed into a cosmopolitan neighbourhood filled with new offices, shops, and restaurants. The lively character of the surroundings, in my experience, adds to the dynamic atmosphere within the office, which reflects the company’s personality and vision.
Workdays at Scigenix officially begin at 7am; however, employees are allowed to start anytime up to 8am, provided they complete the required eight hours of work each day. Additionally, we had the choice to work from home whenever we wished. This flexibility in work hours complemented the relaxed and supportive atmosphere fostered by the company’s leadership, further reinforcing the positive office culture.
Office culture is highly valued at the company, and we often enjoyed social gatherings at the office, particularly on Fridays, when we would have a braai or order takeaway lunches. Practical jokes are also a common occurrence. While this might seem unorthodox in some companies, in my experience, it helped tremendously during afternoons that stretched longer than what a student might otherwise be used to.
The leadership at the company played an integral role in helping me feel welcome from my first day. Shortly after starting my internship and having just moved to Pretoria from Cape Town, I admitted to feeling overwhelmed. I was assured that I should not feel any pressure or experience any stress during my internship and that they were committed to ensuring I had a valuable experience. Small actions such as these are invaluable in helping anyone, and certainly myself, feel welcome at a new organisation. Beyond this, I felt an added level of motivation to do my best, as the support I received inspired me to reciprocate their efforts.

title: Relation to Coursework
text:
Detailed Module Connections

Principles of Statistical Inference
The foundational concepts of hypothesis testing, Type I and Type II errors, and statistical power learned in this module were directly applied when determining sample sizes for clinical trials. Understanding the balance between statistical rigor and practical constraints was crucial for making sound recommendations to study sponsors.


Design and Analysis of Clinical Trials
This module provided the theoretical framework for understanding randomized controlled trials, blinding, allocation concealment, and intention-to-treat analysis. My work on randomisation schedules and participation in Data Safety Committee meetings brought these concepts to life, showing me the real-world complexities of implementing theoretically sound trial designs.


Biostatistical Consulting
The most directly relevant module to my internship. The ASCCR framework (Ask, Structure, Communicate, Clarify, Report), LISA Collaborative Attitude, and POWER structure for collaboration meetings were tools I used regularly. The mock consultations we conducted during the module prepared me well for real client interactions, though I quickly learned that actual consultations require even more flexibility and patience than practice sessions suggested.


Fundamentals of Epidemiology
Understanding study designs, bias, confounding, and effect modification from this module was essential for evaluating the research questions posed by collaborators. The cross-sectional studies I worked on (job satisfaction survey, heart murmur recognition) required careful consideration of the limitations inherent in these designs.


Data Management & Statistical Computing
This module’s emphasis on reproducible research, version control, and good programming practices directly influenced how I structured my analytical work at Scigenix. Every project was developed as a self-contained R package, ensuring transparency and reproducibility—principles heavily emphasized in this module.


Linear Models
The regression techniques learned in this module were foundational for the analyses I conducted. Understanding how to interpret regression coefficients, assess model assumptions, and communicate results in plain language was essential for effective consulting.


Categorical Data Analysis & GLMs
This module was particularly relevant for the job satisfaction survey (ordinal logistic regression for intention to leave) and the fresh gas flow analysis. Understanding when and how to apply these methods was crucial for producing valid results.


Longitudinal Data Analysis
Longitudinal data analysis concepts were applied in projects involving repeated measures such as pharmacokinetic data, where several dozen measurements would be taken on individual participants over time. Techniques for handling correlated observations and missing data were particularly useful.


Analysis of Survival Data
Whilst I did not directly conduct survival analyses during my internship, the principles learned in this module informed my understanding of time-to-event data discussed in clinical trial contexts. This foundational knowledge will be valuable for future projects involving survival outcomes. These concepts were thoroughly applied in my research project as part of my degree.

title: Relation to Coursework
section: From Theory to Practice: Key Insights
text:
From Theory to Practice: Key Insights

The Gap Between Clean Textbook Data and Real-World Messiness
My coursework typically provided clean, well-structured datasets designed to teach specific statistical concepts. The internship exposed me to the reality of incomplete data, inconsistent coding, and variables that don’t behave as expected. Data cleaning often took 50-70% of project time—a reality not always emphasized in coursework.


Statistical Significance vs. Clinical Relevance
Theoretical modules teach us to focus on p-values and confidence intervals. Clinical collaborations taught me that statistical significance means little if the effect size isn’t clinically meaningful. Learning to have these conversations with clinicians was one of the most valuable skills I developed.


The Importance of Communication
Technical skills from my modules were necessary but not sufficient. The ability to explain complex statistical concepts in plain language, to listen carefully to collaborators’ concerns, and to ask clarifying questions proved just as important as knowing which test to run.


Reproducibility in Practice
While coursework emphasized reproducibility in principle, the internship showed me what it means in practice: version-controlled code, comprehensive documentation, validation scripts, and standardized workflows. The R package structure used at Scigenix ensured that analyses could be reproduced months or years later—a critical requirement for regulatory submissions.

Gaps and Areas for Further Development

Regulatory Knowledge
While my statistical training was solid, I realized that understanding regulatory requirements (ICH guidelines, FDA regulations, CDISC standards) is essential for clinical trial work. This is an area where additional formal training would be valuable.


Software Engineering Practices
The Shiny app development project exposed gaps in my knowledge of software engineering principles like unit testing, continuous integration, and deployment. These skills are increasingly important for biostatisticians developing analytical tools.


Medical Terminology
Better familiarity with medical terminology and clinical concepts would have made initial project discussions more efficient. While I picked up relevant terms quickly, a more systematic foundation would have been helpful.

title: Reflection
text:
What Did I Learn?

Technical Skills
The internship solidified and extended my technical statistical knowledge in several ways:
Advanced Data Management My coursework prepared me for analyzing clean datasets, but the internship taught me that data cleaning is often 50-70% of the work. I learned to handle complex data structures (hour-level vs. case-level data), parse messy text fields, and create reproducible data processing pipelines. The fresh gas flow project, in particular, taught me the value of thinking carefully about data structure before diving into analysis.
Production-Grade Programming While I was comfortable with R programming from my coursework, the internship introduced me to software engineering principles for biostatistics. The {golem} framework for Shiny app development, the R package structure for analyses, and the rigorous version control practices at Scigenix showed me what it means to write code that others can trust and maintain years later.
Regulatory Standards Perhaps the most unexpected learning area was the regulatory framework governing clinical research. CDISC standards, MedDRA coding, ICH guidelines—these were barely mentioned in my coursework but proved essential for clinical trial work. Annotating CRFs and developing the coding compliance module gave me practical insight into why these standards exist and how they protect patient safety.


Soft Skills
If I’m honest, the soft skills I developed may prove more valuable than the technical ones:
Communication I learned that explaining statistical concepts clearly is just as important as choosing the right analysis method. The job satisfaction project taught me that “the job is not complete until you can make it understandable.” I practiced translating p-values and confidence intervals into language that clinicians could use to make decisions.
Project Management Managing multiple projects simultaneously, setting weekly goals, tracking deliverables, and coordinating with diverse stakeholders taught me organizational skills that no coursework could provide. I learned to balance perfectionism with pragmatism—knowing when to refine an analysis further and when the current version is good enough to share.
Collaboration The multidisciplinary nature of clinical research means constant collaboration with clinicians, data managers, medical writers, and regulatory specialists. I learned to listen more than I speak, to ask clarifying questions before assuming I understand the problem, and to appreciate that my statistical expertise is just one piece of the puzzle.
Resilience Not every analysis goes smoothly. Data doesn’t always behave as expected. Collaborators sometimes request changes that feel unnecessary. I learned to view setbacks as learning opportunities rather than failures, and to maintain professional composure even when frustrated.

title: Reflection
text:
Why Was This Learning Significant?

Bridging the Theory-Practice Gap
My MSc coursework provided an excellent theoretical foundation, but the internship showed me how to apply that knowledge in messy, real-world situations. Understanding the difference between statistical significance and clinical relevance, between a perfect analysis and a timely one, between what the textbook says and what actually works—these insights are what transform a student into a practitioner.


Understanding the Bigger Picture
Before the internship, I thought about statistics in isolation—choose a test, run it, interpret the results. Now I understand that statistical analysis sits within a complex ecosystem: research ethics, regulatory requirements, patient safety, budget constraints, timeline pressures, and organizational politics. Seeing this broader context has made me a more thoughtful and effective biostatistician.


Career Direction
The internship confirmed that I want to pursue a career in clinical research biostatistics. Seeing the tangible impact of statistical work on patient care—whether through the heart murmur study potentially improving pre-operative assessments or the fresh gas flow analysis contributing to environmental responsibility—gave me a sense of purpose that theoretical coursework couldn’t provide.


Professional Identity
I entered the internship as a student learning biostatistics. I’m leaving as a biostatistician who happens to still be completing formal studies. This shift in identity—from student to professional—may sound subtle, but it has profoundly affected how I approach problems, communicate with colleagues, and think about my career.

title: Reflection
section: What Would I Have Done Differently?
text:
What Would I Have Done Differently?

Earlier Engagement with Medical Terminology
Looking back, I wish I had spent time before the internship familiarizing myself with basic medical terminology and clinical concepts. While I picked up necessary terms quickly during projects, having this foundation from the start would have made initial discussions more efficient and reduced the cognitive load when learning new statistical methods simultaneously.


More Proactive Questions
In the early weeks, I sometimes hesitated to ask questions for fear of appearing incompetent. I now realize that asking clarifying questions early saves time later and demonstrates professional maturity rather than weakness. If I could do it again, I would be more proactive in seeking clarification when project requirements were ambiguous.


Systematic Documentation from Day One
While I maintained good documentation throughout the internship, I wish I had been even more systematic from the beginning. Keeping a daily log of what I learned, challenges I faced, and solutions I discovered would have made this reflection easier to write and would provide valuable reference material for future projects.


Time Management for Reflective Practice
The intensity of project work sometimes meant that reflection happened only when required (like for this portfolio). Building in regular time for reflection; perhaps 30 minutes every Friday afternoon—would have deepened my learning in real-time rather than retrospectively.

title: Reflection
section: Challenges Encountered and How I Handled Them
text:
Challenges Encountered and How I Handled Them

Challenge 1: Imposter Syndrome
The Challenge: Especially in the first month, I felt overwhelmed by how much I didn’t know. Experienced colleagues seemed to navigate complex regulatory requirements and statistical challenges effortlessly, while I struggled with basic concepts like CDISC domains.
How I Handled It: I reminded myself that comparing my beginning to their middle wasn’t fair. I focused on daily progress rather than absolute expertise. I also found that being honest about what I didn’t know—rather than pretending—actually built trust with colleagues who appreciated my willingness to learn.
What I Learned: Everyone was once a beginner. Expertise comes from experience, not from innate talent. Being comfortable with not knowing everything is actually a sign of professional maturity.


Challenge 2: Balancing Multiple Projects
The Challenge: At one point, I was simultaneously working on the job satisfaction analysis, developing the Shiny app, and learning about manual edit checks. The context-switching was exhausting and I worried about doing justice to any single project.
How I Handled It: I implemented time-blocking—dedicating specific days or half-days to specific projects rather than trying to make progress on everything simultaneously. I also communicated more proactively with my supervisor about realistic timelines.
What I Learned: Saying no (or “not yet”) is sometimes the most professional response. Clear communication about capacity prevents over-commitment and under-delivery.


Challenge 3: Technical Obstacles with Real Consequences
The Challenge: When working on the manual edit checks, I encountered validation rules that seemed to produce false positives. Unlike coursework where errors are academic, these errors could delay a clinical trial or, worse, allow invalid data to proceed.
How I Handled It: Rather than assuming my code was correct, I systematically tested edge cases, consulted documentation, and when still uncertain, brought specific examples to senior colleagues for review. I learned to value thoroughness over speed.
What I Learned: In clinical research, being approximately right is not good enough. The stakes—patient safety, regulatory compliance, company reputation—demand precision. This isn’t perfectionism; it’s professionalism.


Challenge 4: Navigating Stakeholder Disagreements
The Challenge: During the job satisfaction project meeting, the researcher and their supervisors had different views on how results should be presented. As the statistician, I was caught in the middle of competing preferences.
How I Handled It: I focused on statistical principles and evidence-based practice rather than personal preferences. I provided options when multiple approaches were defensible, clearly explaining the trade-offs. I remained neutral and professional, positioning myself as an expert advisor rather than an advocate for any particular stakeholder.
What I Learned: The statistician’s role is often to facilitate evidence-based decision-making, not to make decisions unilaterally. Understanding group dynamics and maintaining professional neutrality are important skills.


Challenge 5: The Pace of Industry vs. Academia
The Challenge: I was accustomed to academic timelines where thorough exploration of methods is valued. At Scigenix, project timelines were often tight, and “good enough” sometimes had to suffice when “perfect” wasn’t feasible.
How I Handled It: I learned to prioritize—which aspects of an analysis were critical to get exactly right (e.g., primary outcomes, regulatory requirements) vs. which were less critical (e.g., exploratory subgroup analyses). I also got better at scoping projects realistically upfront.
What I Learned: Perfect is the enemy of good. In industry, delivering a solid analysis on time is more valuable than delivering a perfect analysis too late. This doesn’t mean compromising on quality for core analyses, but it does mean being strategic about where to invest effort.

title: Reflection
text:
Overall Reflections

The Most Important Lesson
If I had to distill the internship into one lesson, it would be this: Biostatistics is fundamentally a people discipline, not just a technical discipline. The statistical methods matter, of course, but success depends on understanding what collaborators need, communicating clearly, managing expectations, and building trust. The best analysis in the world is worthless if you can’t explain it in a way that enables decision-making.


Gratitude
I am deeply grateful to Scigenix for taking a chance on a student with limited practical experience. The supportive culture, excellent mentorship from Dr. Swart and other colleagues, and the diversity of projects I was exposed to exceeded my expectations. The company’s commitment to scientific excellence while maintaining a genuinely enjoyable work environment set a standard I will carry forward in my career.


Looking Forward
As I complete my MSc and look toward my career, the internship has given me clarity about what I want from professional life:

Work that has tangible impact on patient care and public health
Collaborative environments where statistical expertise is valued and integrated into decision-making
Opportunities for continuous learning and technical growth
Organizations that balance scientific rigor with supportive culture

I’m excited to take the skills, knowledge, and professional identity I’ve developed at Scigenix into the next chapter of my career.

Description of Activities
According to module_timetable.pdf (Block 1 – 19 May), we introduced ASCCR, practiced the POWER structure for consultations, and grounded the day in reflective practice using structured frameworks (Gibbs, Kolb, Mezirow). Short role-plays emphasized intentional openings and shared outcomes.

title: Week 2, Day 1
text:
Reflection (Gibbs Reflective Cycle)

1. Description
We mapped ASCCR onto real consultations and practiced POWER—Purpose, Orientation, Work plan, Expectations, and Review—to create momentum and accountability. Reflection frameworks were presented as tools to convert experience into growth rather than post-hoc journaling.


2. Feelings
I felt relief at having a unifying scaffold; previous consultations felt improvisational. POWER made openings less awkward and endings more decisive. The reflective writing piece felt both familiar and newly practical when framed as an iterative learning engine.


3. Evaluation
ASCCR’s clarity helped me diagnose past friction points (unclear roles; mismatched expectations). POWER translated those insights into behaviors. The role-plays surfaced micro-skills (paraphrasing, timeboxing, agenda setting) I often underuse. I wanted more feedback on my tone and pacing.


4. Analysis
Kolb’s cycle justifies short learning loops: plan, act, reflect, refine. Mezirow’s critical reflection surfaced assumptions (e.g., “jump to methods quickly shows competence”); double-loop learning encouraged replacing them with “align on purpose and constraints first.” ASCCR works as a diagnostic: if a conversation derails, I can ask which letter is weak.


5. Conclusion
Consultations improve when I choreograph them: purposeful openings, explicit scope, co-authored next steps, and deliberate closings. Reflection is not separate from practice—it is the practice that improves practice.


6. Action Plan
I will use a one-page POWER opener, an ASCCR checklist for debriefs, and 10-minute post-meeting notes (Gibbs prompts). I will solicit feedback from collaborators on clarity of purpose and action items to calibrate my delivery.

title: Week 2, Day 2
text:
Reflection (Gibbs Reflective Cycle)

1. Description
We operationalized the LISA attitude—service-oriented, respectful, and empowering—through structured meetings and role-plays. We reviewed co-authorship norms and used analogies to translate complex ideas into shared language.


2. Feelings
I felt grounded by the clarity of behavioral cues (how to show respect, curiosity, and care). Discussing co-authorship reduced ambiguity I’ve felt around credit and accountability. Role-play was uncomfortable at first, then freeing as muscle memory formed.


3. Evaluation
The combination of attitude, structure, and practice worked. The LISA lens made small behaviors matter (greetings, agenda co-creation, follow-through). Co-authorship guidance was actionable—memos at project start prevent later conflict. Analogies improved clarity without losing rigor.


4. Analysis
ASCCR connects here: Attitude and Relationship are not soft extras; they are the context that makes Content persuasive and Communication effective. Mezirow’s lens surfaced my assumption that “writing authorship later is harmless”—a risky belief. Double-loop learning prompts me to address roles early as part of Structure.


5. Conclusion
Relationship-first doesn’t mean method-second; it means method-with-purpose. Clear roles and collaborative behaviors reduce friction and raise trust, enabling better science.


6. Action Plan
I will implement a standard opening (greeting, purpose, agenda, time), use a brief authorship/roles memo for new projects, and maintain an analogies bank for recurring explanations. I’ll request explicit feedback on how my behaviors support a collaborative atmosphere.

On 17 April (Block 2), the day focused on determinants of a successful career, writing statistical sections in protocols/papers/SAPs, reporting studies in health, and a session on ethics and scientific integrity. title: Week 1, Day 4
text:
Reflection (Gibbs Reflective Cycle)

1. Description
We connected career sustainability with everyday technical choices: writing statistical sections that are clear and defensible, applying reporting guidance consistently, and foregrounding ethics and integrity. The sessions positioned integrity as a daily practice, not a periodic audit.


2. Feelings
I felt inspired by the clarity of what “professional” looks like in our field and sobered by how easily shortcuts can erode trust. The emphasis on writing statistical sections gave me confidence—structure can be learned and reused.


3. Evaluation
The integration of career determinants with writing and reporting was effective: reputation emerges from repeated, transparent practices. The ethics session made abstract principles concrete through realistic dilemmas (authorship, analytic flexibility, timeline pressure). More time on authorship negotiation would have helped.


4. Analysis
Using ASCCR: Attitude (integrity and humility), Structure (clear scope, roles, authorship), Content (pre-specified estimands and justified methods), Communication (transparent assumptions and limitations), Relationship (trust via reliability). Mezirow’s lens reframed “success” from output volume to trustworthy influence. Double-loop learning challenged my assumptions about deadlines—quality and clarity are non-negotiable.


5. Conclusion
Career durability rests on ethical consistency, reproducible documentation, and reader-centered statistical sections. Reporting guidance is not bureaucracy—it is the language of credibility.


6. Action Plan
I will adopt authorship/roles memos at project start, maintain SAP templates with rationale sections, and apply reporting checklists systematically. I’ll keep an “integrity log” for analytic decisions and schedule periodic assumption checks with collaborators.

title: Week 1, Day 3
text:
Reflection (Gibbs Reflective Cycle)

1. Description
We practiced teaching collaborators how to work with statisticians, reviewed principles for reporting science, and learned to frame researchable questions that connect purpose, design, and estimand. The sessions stressed reciprocity in education and transparency in methods and documentation.


2. Feelings
I felt encouraged that teaching is a learnable craft and relieved to have concrete approaches for difficult explanations. The reporting discussion heightened my sense of responsibility; small documentation choices can materially affect replicability and trust.


3. Evaluation
The bidirectional model (learn their clinical world; teach statistical thinking) felt practical and respectful. Reporting guidance was actionable—checklists and exemplars clarified expectations. I wished for more time to practice reframing vague questions into answerable ones with stakeholders in the room.


4. Analysis
ASCCR guided me to center Communication and Relationship: listening precedes explaining; partnership outruns service. Kolb’s cycle suggests repeated, low-stakes practice to internalize teaching skills. Double-loop learning shifted me from solution-first to question-first: if the question is mis-specified, excellent analysis still disappoints. Clear reporting operationalizes integrity.


5. Conclusion
Teaching, framing questions, and reporting are mutually reinforcing. They move collaborations from transactions to co-creation, anchoring rigor in shared understanding and transparent documentation.


6. Action Plan
I will prepare analogies and visuals for common concepts, adopt a reproducibility/reporting checklist, and develop a short “question-framing” guide (purpose, estimand, outcomes, design, constraints). I’ll schedule pre-meet reads of clinical background to align language and goals.

Description of Activities
On 15 April (Block 2), we examined strategies for successful proposals and manuscripts, learned from a senior biostatistician’s career journey, and reviewed frequent errors in RCTs (design, analysis, and interpretation). The day emphasized writing as a professional lever, linking technical rigor with persuasive, ethical communication.

title: Week 1, Day 2
text:
Reflection (Gibbs Reflective Cycle)

1. Description
We connected scientific writing craft with career strategy and trial methodology. The writing session offered practical templates for proposals and manuscripts. The career talk illuminated pathways, trade-offs, and serendipity. The RCT errors review highlighted design and analysis pitfalls that undermine validity and credibility.


2. Feelings
Initially, I felt daunted by the gap between my current writing and fundable, publishable prose. Hearing an honest career narrative was both motivating and grounding. The RCT examples produced a healthy unease—how easily well-intentioned choices can bias results.


3. Evaluation
What worked was the tight coupling of writing (how we argue), career development (why we invest), and methodology (what we defend). The balance of exemplars and checklists made the guidance actionable. I would have benefited from more time to practice rewriting weak paragraphs with peer feedback.


4. Analysis
ASCCR sharpened my lens: Content is not only correct but convincing; Communication is audience-centered; Relationship includes co-authorship norms and accountability. Kolb’s cycle applies—draft, reflect, revise, redeploy. Double-loop learning reframed “good writing” from correctness to reader impact and ethical clarity. RCT pitfalls reinforced the need for preregistered structure and transparent reporting.


5. Conclusion
Strong writing is a force multiplier for biostatistical impact; it carries methods into decisions. Career growth is cumulative—skills, networks, and artifacts (protocols, grants) co-evolve. Vigilance against RCT errors protects scientific integrity and public trust.


6. Action Plan
I will implement weekly writing sprints, adopt a lab style guide, and maintain proposal/manuscript templates. I’ll pilot a pre-submission checklist covering design clarity, estimand alignment, and reporting standards. I’ll schedule quarterly career reflections and seek targeted mentorship on grant strategy.

On 14 April (Block 2), the day covered our role in collaborations, the Biostatistician’s Code of Conduct, practical tips for enhancing collaborations, and mentorship in academia. Complementary sessions focused on communicating statistics to clinicians, avoiding misuse of statistical language and methods, and contrasting statistical significance with clinical relevance in interventional research.

title: Week 1, Day 1
text:
Reflection (Gibbs Reflective Cycle)

1. Description
Today established my professional identity beyond “data analyst”: collaborator, educator, and ethical steward. We explored the Code of Conduct, strategies for enhancing collaborations, mentorship as a lever for growth, how to communicate statistics to clinicians, and how statistical significance differs from clinical importance. The sessions collectively framed collaboration as an ethically bounded, communication-intensive practice.


2. Feelings
I felt energized by the expanded view of my role, yet humbled by the ethical weight of biostatistical advice. The communication sessions were reassuring—clarity is a skill I can deliberately practice. Mentorship sparked motivation, with a trace of anxiety about initiating relationships respectfully and productively.


3. Evaluation
The day’s coherence stood out: ethics set guardrails; collaboration tips translated principles into practice; communication and language guidance improved precision; mentorship offered a sustainable development pathway. A minor limitation was limited time to interrogate nuanced dilemmas (e.g., balancing collaborator timelines with analytic rigor).


4. Analysis
Using ASCCR, I reframed practice: Attitude (service, humility), Structure (clear expectations and authorship), Content (co-created questions), Communication (bidirectional and jargon-aware), Relationship (trust over time). Mezirow’s critical reflection surfaced a prior assumption that my value is mainly technical; today challenged that. Kolb’s cycle was evident—experience, reflection, principles, and planned experimentation. Double-loop learning applies: not just doing analyses better, but redefining “good” as ethically sound and clinically meaningful.


5. Conclusion
I learned that effective collaboration integrates ethical judgment, relational competence, and translational communication. Technical accuracy is necessary but insufficient; meaning-making with clinicians is the bridge from numbers to impact.


6. Action Plan
I will create a personal conduct checklist (conflicts, authorship, reproducibility), adopt POWER-style openings for meetings, and maintain a terminology watchlist to avoid common misuse. I’ll identify two mentors and prepare specific, value-respecting questions. I’ll schedule monthly double-loop reflections to examine assumptions about my role and the clinical relevance of my recommendations.

The Gibbs Reflective Cycle
All reflections in this section are structured according to Graham Gibbs’ (1988) six-stage reflective cycle:

Description: What happened during the session(s)?
Feelings: What was I thinking and feeling?
Evaluation: What was good and bad about the experience?
Analysis: What sense can I make of the situation?
Conclusion: What did I learn from this experience?
Action Plan: What will I do differently next time?

This framework ensures that my reflections move beyond simple description to critical analysis and actionable insights for professional development.

1. Description
We practiced questioning as the engine of collaboration—clarifying purpose, success criteria, data realities, and constraints—then ran complete consultations with peer feedback. We converted conversations into written summaries that make decisions auditable.


2. Feelings
Initially I felt stretched—balancing deep listening with structured probing. As the day progressed, the flow improved: questions scaffolded empathy and rigor at the same time. Writing the summaries sharpened thinking.

The question sets reduced rework by exposing hidden assumptions early. Integrated practice surfaced small but costly habits (vague action items, missing timelines). Documentation locked in shared understanding and facilitated next steps.

ASCCR highlights that strong Content emerges from shared framing; questioning is how we co-create that frame. Kolb’s cycle explains the benefit of immediate reflection and revision. Double-loop learning challenged my bias to “answer quickly”; better questions improved both efficiency and trust.


5. Conclusion
Great consulting is great questioning tied to disciplined follow-through. When questions align purpose, estimand, and design, downstream analyses and writing become smoother and more defensible.


6. Action Plan
I will maintain a questioning script (objectives, estimand, outcomes, design, constraints), an action-item template with owners/dates, and a one-page consultation summary format. I’ll schedule a monthly peer review of my consultation notes for calibration.

1. Job Satisfaction Survey Analysis

Project Overview
One of the main statistical consulting projects I worked on during my internship involved analysing a job satisfaction survey among anaesthesia consultants and registrars in South Africa. The purpose of the study was to assess key domains of job satisfaction using the Minnesota Satisfaction Questionnaire (MSQ). We also wanted to explore how satisfaction, demographic variables, and respondents’ intention to leave their current post were associated.


My Responsibilities
My responsibilities covered the full spectrum of statistical support:

Data Management: Imported raw Excel data into R, cleaned and recoded over sixty variables, with particular attention to managing Likert-scale responses, multi-select questions, and missing values
Psychometric Assessment: Implemented scoring framework for MSQ capturing intrinsic, extrinsic, and general satisfaction domains; assessed internal consistency using Cronbach’s alpha; conducted exploratory factor analysis to examine dimensional structure
Statistical Analysis: Used both parametric and non-parametric methods to compare satisfaction scores between consultants and registrars; employed ordinal logistic regression to model intention to leave as a function of demographic predictors
Reporting: Produced comprehensive demographic tables, publication-quality summary tables, and clear visualizations (histograms, boxplots, and Likert plots)



Key Challenges and Learning
A key outcome of the study was to determine whether factors like age and gender were associated with anaesthesiologists’ intention to leave. I used ordinal logistic regression for this. While the computational aspects in R were familiar, interpreting the results in understandable language proved challenging, particularly since this method was new to me. My supervisor encouraged me to make the findings understandable to clinicians. After several attempts, I learned a valuable lesson: “the job is not complete until you can make it understandable.”


Consultation Meeting Experience
This project involved a meeting with the researcher, their two supervisors, and my internship supervisor. Having completed a mock consultation for my degree’s Biostatistical Consulting module, I felt prepared, but the reality was different. I spent the day expecting questions about the regression or ANOVA results. However, much of the meeting focused on stylistic aspects of the report, such as adjusting axis font sizes on graphs or selecting density plots instead of histograms.
This experience exposed me to the realities of working within a multidisciplinary team. I realised that much of my time would be spent refining report details to ensure clarity and acceptability for journal submission, rather than focusing solely on statistical analysis. While this initially felt frustrating, I grew to appreciate the collaborative process of generating new knowledge.


Skills Developed

Project management (weekly goal-setting for data cleaning and analysis)
Independent research on best practices for interpreting ordinal logistic regression
Personal quality control and document tracking
Regular communication with team members to keep project on track

2. Can Anaesthesiology Trainees Distinguish Between Different Heart Murmurs?

Project Overview
This cross-sectional study investigated whether anaesthesiology trainees could distinguish between benign and pathologic paediatric heart murmurs using pre-recorded audio clips. The project addressed the ability of anaesthetists to identify pathologic murmurs during pre-operative assessments, which directly affects patient safety and theatre efficiency. Participants completed a 20-question online test (MurmurQuiz) and provided background information relating to their clinical experience.


My Responsibilities

Data Management: Developed a modular, reproducible codebase in R that processed raw quiz results and survey data, performed data cleaning, derived performance classifications, and merged relevant covariates
Descriptive Analysis: Produced visual summaries (boxplots) and descriptive tables to explore patterns in test accuracy across experience-related factors
Regression Modeling: Conducted both univariate and multivariable logistic regression analyses to assess associations between clinical experience and murmur recognition performance
Reporting: Summarized models in well-formatted tables using the gtsummary package, enabling easy interpretation by non-statistical stakeholders



Personal Significance
I found this project particularly rewarding since it had hints of educational research. The overarching theme was to determine how capable trainees are at doing routine yet incredibly important tasks. Beyond this, the fact that the work was focused on paediatric patients specifically gave me a sense of personal satisfaction knowing that the work I was doing could have real-world impact on quality of care provided to some of our most vulnerable patients.


Skills Developed

Development of modular, reproducible analytical code
Integration of data from multiple sources (quiz performance and demographic surveys)
Application of logistic regression for educational research questions
Creation of stakeholder-friendly reports using modern R packages

3. Analysis of Fresh Gas Flow Rates

Project Overview
The “Analysis of Fresh Gas Flow Rates and its Effect on Consumption and Cost of Inhalational Anaesthetic Agents in a Tertiary Academic Hospital in Pretoria” was both one of the most challenging and impactful projects of my internship. Motivated by the growing recognition of climate change and healthcare’s responsibility to address its environmental footprint, this study aimed to examine current anaesthetic practices—specifically, the use of volatile inhalational agents and nitrous oxide, both notable greenhouse gases.


Data Structure Challenges
Initial data cleaning was challenging due to the large volume of data that needed analysis. The raw dataset had information at various levels: one set at the case level and another at the hour level. To streamline the workflow and align with the study’s objectives, I created two separate datasets, one representing each level, before “mapping” variables between them.
A particular obstacle related to how clinicians were represented in the original files. Instead of having each clinician in a separate column, the data stored all names for a given case in a single cell, separated by commas. To address this, I wrote a script in R that parsed the clinician column, split the names by commas, and assigned each name to a new column.


Statistical Approach
After cleaning and restructuring the data, I matched variables across the two datasets to facilitate analysis. The analysis included:

Calculating summary statistics
Generating visualizations
Applying a generalized linear model to account for clinicians who worked on multiple cases



Impact and Insights
This project highlighted the importance of well-thought-out data cleaning and documentation, as well as the value of robust, reproducible code for complex analyses. Importantly, by identifying patterns in anaesthetic agent usage and their associated costs, the findings offer actionable insights that could help reduce the hospital’s carbon footprint and promote environmentally responsible healthcare practices.


Skills Developed

Advanced data restructuring and manipulation in R
String parsing and data extraction from complex formats
Generalized linear modeling for clustered data
Environmental impact assessment in healthcare settings

4. Randomisation

Overview
As the name suggests, randomisation is a principal component of any Randomised Controlled Trial (RCT). Randomly assigning treatment ensures that a participant’s potential health outcomes do not influence the allocation process. This approach makes the treatment groups comparable on average, even with respect to unmeasured confounders. Consequently, comparing outcomes by assigned group yields an unbiased estimate of the treatment’s causal effect.


My Contribution
Being asked to prepare a randomisation schedule was an exciting opportunity, particularly as the topic had not been covered in depth during my MSc. Completing this task gave me a keen sense of accomplishment, as it marked my first concrete contribution to a clinical trial.


Technical Implementation
An especially interesting aspect was the division of the process into two stages:

Mock Randomisation: Employed a fixed random seed to ensure reproducibility for validation purposes
Final Randomisation: Used a randomly selected seed between 1 and 2 million (excluding the mock seed) to generate the actual allocation sequence

While these were mathematically and programmatically identical, this two-stage process ensured both reproducibility (for quality control) and true randomness (for the actual trial).


Skills Developed

Understanding of different randomisation methods (simple, blocked, stratified)
Programming techniques in R to ensure true randomness
Regulatory procedures for generating and documenting randomisation sequences
Appreciation for the rigour needed in clinical trials

5. Data Safety Committee

Background and Motivation
I am particularly interested in the crucial role that ethics plays in clinical research. Since beginning my journey in public health, I have come to regard ethical research practices as a fundamental part upon which the entire research process is built. I dedicated many hours to understanding the Declaration of Helsinki, the lasting infamy of the Tuskegee Syphilis Study, and the role of safety review committees in clinical trials.


Scigenix’s Commitment to Ethics
This emphasis on ethics became especially clear during my internship at Scigenix. From the start, Scigenix demonstrated a deep commitment to patient wellbeing. I was encouraged to approach the clinical research process holistically, always remembering that our goal is to improve people’s lives. In biostatistics, our work is often far removed from patients (both physically and metaphorically) which can make it easy to forget the individuals behind the numbers and graphs. To address this, the company enrolled all staff in an intensive Good Clinical Practice (GCP) training course.


Data Safety Committee Meeting
One of my goals going into this internship was to attend a Data Safety Review Committee meeting. These committees are tasked with scrutinising clinical trial conduct, evaluating results, and safeguarding patient safety. Although they play an integral role in research, many young biostatisticians perceive them as mysterious, since participating requires substantial clinical trial experience.
While the meeting itself was strictly confidential, I was able to see firsthand that there was zero tolerance for anything that might put study participants at risk. Notably, I found it interesting that decisions on whether to continue a study were made formally through voting.


Learning Outcomes

Understanding of the role and function of Data Safety Monitoring Boards
Appreciation for the ethical responsibilities of biostatisticians
Insight into formal decision-making processes in clinical trials
Reinforcement of patient-centered approach to research

text:
6. Quality Control

The Standard of Excellence
In clinical research, the expectation is that all work produced, whether statistical outputs, tables, figures, or reports, is of the highest standard and as close to flawless as possible. This standard is not simply aspirational but essential, given the regulatory and ethical stakes involved in trial reporting.


QC Process Implementation
To achieve this level of rigour, we employed a structured quality control process grounded in peer review and accountability. Specifically, we used a comprehensive checklist system developed in Excel, where team members took responsibility for reviewing a colleague’s work line by line.
Each item on the checklist targeted a specific aspect of quality:

Correct application of statistical methods
Alignment between R outputs and their presentation in Word
Compliance with pre-specified templates and reporting conventions

No detail was considered too minor to call for attention. Stylistic consistency such as the use of decimal points, abbreviations, and font sizing was meticulously checked. Figures were assessed for readability, clarity, and adherence to visual standards. Even elements like axis labels, colour schemes, and legend placement were scrutinised to ensure they communicated information effectively and professionally.


Insights Gained
This process highlighted the importance of collaborative vigilance and instilled in me a deep respect for the behind-the-scenes discipline that underpins transparent and reproducible research. It also reinforced the notion that producing statistically valid results is only one part of the job—communicating them clearly and accurately is equally critical.

text:
7. Annotated Case Report Forms

Introduction to CDISC Standards
One of the most eye-opening tasks during my internship was working on annotated Case Report Forms (CRFs). Before starting this work, I had only a theoretical understanding of how clinical trial data gets organized and standardized. What I discovered was a world of detail that makes my earlier coursework seem refreshingly straightforward by comparison.


The Task
The basic premise seemed simple enough: take the forms used to collect patient data during clinical trials and figure out where each piece of information should go according to CDISC SDTM (Study Data Tabulation Model) standards. In practice, this meant looking at everything from basic demographic questions to complex adverse event reporting and deciding which standardized “domain” each variable belonged to.


The Complexity
Working through these domain mappings quickly taught me that what appears obvious often is not. A simple question about a patient’s medical history might seem like it clearly belongs in the Medical History (MH) domain, but depending on when it was collected and how it relates to the study, it could potentially fit elsewhere. I found myself constantly referring to CDISC implementation guides, trying to decode the logic behind these classification systems.


Broader Impact
What struck me most about this experience was how it illuminated the incredible infrastructure supporting modern clinical research. Before this internship, I understood clinical trials primarily through the lens of statistical analysis. Working on CRF annotations revealed the enormous effort required just to ensure that data can be collected, organized, and submitted in ways that regulatory agencies can review and approve.
This work also gave me a new appreciation for the tedious regulatory requirements that govern clinical research. What initially appeared to be bureaucratic complications revealed themselves as essential safeguards ensuring that clinical trial data can be trusted, compared across studies, and used to make important decisions about drug safety and efficacy.

title: Work Outputs
text:
8. Manual Edit Checks

Overview
One of the most involved experiences during my internship involved working on the Manual Edit Check (MEC) process for a clinical trial. What initially appeared to be a straightforward data validation exercise quickly revealed itself as a sophisticated quality assurance framework that underpins the integrity of clinical research.


Scope of the MEC Process
The MEC process for the study encompassed 134 unique validation rules spanning the entire clinical data lifecycle. These checks were systematically categorized into:

Clinical (CLIN) checks: Focused on clinical logic and medical plausibility
Listing (LIS) checks: Focused on data completeness and consistency

The sheer scope of this validation framework was initially overwhelming, particularly given that my earlier exposure to data quality control had been limited to basic data cleaning exercises in coursework.


Technical Implementation
My primary responsibility involved implementing and refining the R-based validation framework that executed these checks automatically. Each validation rule required translation into a dedicated R function that would examine specific data elements and return standardized results:

PASS: Data meeting all criteria
FAIL: Definitive errors requiring correction
REVIEW: Cases demanding manual evaluation



Complex Validation Logic
The most intellectually stimulating aspect was working with the Inclusion/Exclusion criteria checks, which made up a large chunk of the total validation rules. These checks required sophisticated logic to manage scenarios such as specific medical events during the study period—cases where participants initially meeting eligibility criteria might experience status changes that affected their continued participation.
The cross-form validation components proved particularly challenging, as they demanded integration of data from multiple CRF domains to ensure consistency. For instance, confirming that adverse event onset dates aligned with visit dates required matching temporal data across different forms while accounting for potential data entry variations and protocol-defined visit windows.


Impact on Understanding
Working on this project fundamentally changed my appreciation for the infrastructure supporting clinical research. Before this experience, I understood clinical trials primarily through the lens of statistical analysis and study design. The MEC process revealed the enormous effort needed to ensure that data can be trusted for regulatory submissions—an aspect of biostatistical work that receives little attention in academic coursework but proves essential in practice.

title: Work Outputs
text:
9. Shiny App Development

Project Overview
During the latter phase of my internship, I undertook what would become one of the most technically challenging and professionally rewarding projects: developing a production-grade Shiny application for comparing clinical trial datasets and validating medical coding compliance.


Business Need
This project emerged from a dual need within Scigenix’s quality assurance workflow:

Data Validation: The ability to efficiently validate data consistency across various stages of clinical trial data processing, particularly during database lock procedures that precede regulatory submissions
Coding Compliance: Ensuring accurate medical coding using current MedDRA (Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities)



Technical Architecture
The application’s core functionality centred on two complementary validation processes:

Dataset Comparison Module

Implemented using the Arsenal package’s comparedf() function in R
Designed to identify discrepancies that could affect trial integrity
Capable of handling large clinical datasets with multiple data domains



Coding Checks Module

Validates medical terminology across three critical domains:

Adverse Events (AE)
Medical History (MH)
Concomitant Medications (CM)

Ensures all medical terms coded using current dictionary versions
Validates LLT_CURRENCY (Lowest Level Term Currency) to guarantee regulatory compliance with MedDRA standards




Development Approach
My approach to development followed the {golem} framework, an R package that simplifies the creation and deployment of production-ready Shiny apps. I came to appreciate this framework for its emphasis on:

Production readiness
Software development best practices
Modular architecture

I structured the full application using smaller Shiny “modules”—one for data comparison and another for coding checks—a process akin to “eating an elephant bit-by-bit.” The coding module required particular attention to dictionary management, as it needed to interface with multiple MedDRA versions and WHO Drug dictionaries stored on the company’s SharePoint system.


Lessons Learned
Reflecting on this experience, I realize how it synthesized everything I had learned during my MSc while simultaneously exposing me to entirely new domains of knowledge. The project required not just statistical and programming expertise, but also an understanding of:

Clinical research processes
Medical coding standards
Regulatory requirements
Enterprise software development practices

The gap between academic programming and production-grade software became starkly apparent. Where my coursework emphasized getting the right answer, this project demanded getting the right answer reliably, reproducibly, and verifiably, with comprehensive documentation of every decision.


Impact
The most valuable lesson from this project was understanding how biostatisticians can contribute beyond traditional analysis roles. By developing tools that enhance both data quality and coding compliance while streamlining validation processes, we can multiply our impact across entire research programs. This application will save Scigenix several hours per study in data validation and coding verification time while reducing error rates—a tangible contribution to improving clinical research efficiency and regulatory compliance.

How I Met Each Learning Outcome

Sample Size Determination
Through my work on randomisation for clinical trials, I applied mock power calculations and sample size determination for RCTs. This helped me understand Type I and Type II errors and their practical implications in trial design. I learned to balance statistical power with practical constraints such as budget, timeline, and recruitment feasibility.


Statistical Analysis Plan Development
I developed comprehensive analysis plans for multiple consultation projects, specifying primary and secondary outcomes, statistical methods, and approaches for handling missing data. This skill was particularly important for ensuring reproducibility and transparency in research findings.


Formulating Research Questions
I worked closely with clinical researchers to translate their clinical problems into testable statistical hypotheses. This required ensuring that research questions were specific, measurable, and aligned with available data. The job satisfaction survey and heart murmur studies provided excellent opportunities to practice this skill.


Questionnaire Design
I gained experience working with validated instruments like the Minnesota Satisfaction Questionnaire (MSQ) and contributed to the design of the MurmurQuiz. This taught me about Likert scales, response bias, and validation measures. This also introduced me to the concept of ordinal logistic regression, which is an often misunderstood statistical method due to its complexity in terms of interpreting results.


Formulating Study Designs
My contributions to RCT design through randomisation schedules helped me understand the importance of proper study design. I also gained insight into cross-sectional and observational study limitations through the consultation projects.


Communication – Oral and Written
Throughout my internship, I regularly presented findings to colleagues and collaborators from consulting project. This was perhaps the most frequently exercised skill, as every project required clear communication with non-statistical stakeholders.


Research Ethics
My participation in the Data Safety Committee and completion of Good Clinical Practice (GCP) training deepened my understanding of the Declaration of Helsinki principles in practice. I learned that ethical research practices form the foundation upon which all clinical research must be built.


Data Management
I performed extensive data cleaning in R and managed complex datasets with both hour-level and case-level data structures. Creating reproducible workflows was essential for maintaining data integrity and enabling quality control.


Quality Control
I implemented peer review processes using Excel checklists for QC and ensured regulatory compliance in all outputs. This taught me that producing statistically valid results is only part of the job—communicating them clearly and accurately is equally critical.


Advanced Statistical Programming
I developed R packages for analyses, created automated reporting systems, and implemented complex data transformations and modeling. The Shiny app development project, in particular, challenged me to integrate multiple programming skills to create a production-ready tool.


Collaboration
Working effectively within multidisciplinary teams including clinicians, data managers, and regulatory specialists was a daily requirement. I learned the importance of listening, asking clarifying questions, and finding common ground when technical and clinical perspectives diverged.


Consulting Skills
I led consultation meetings, translated clinical questions into statistical problems, and provided actionable recommendations. The mock consultation from the BC module prepared me well, but real-world consultations taught me that flexibility and patience are just as important as technical expertise.


Leadership Skills
On the job satisfaction survey project, I took ownership of the analysis, managed project timelines, and coordinated with multiple researchers. This experience showed me that leadership in biostatistics often means guiding the analytical process while empowering collaborators to make informed decisions.


Statistical Analysis
I applied a wide range of statistical methods including logistic regression, ordinal logistic regression, various hypothesis tests, and factor analysis. Managing Likert scale data taught me the importance of choosing appropriate methods for the data structure and research question.

title: Design and report simulation studies the smart way with ADEMP
section: Simulation study = a virtual experiment on data
text:
Simulation study = a virtual experiment on data






A simulation study is essentially a controlled experiment where we know the truth from the start. Think of it as three key steps:

We create data where we control the parameters—we set the true effect size, sample size, variability, etc.
We apply methods to that data—the same statistical methods we’d use in practice (regression, tests, estimation techniques).
We evaluate performance** by comparing results against the known truth—measuring bias, coverage, power, and other metrics.

This gives us complete transparency: we can see exactly when methods work well, when they start to break down, and under what conditions they fail entirely.

title: Design and report simulation studies the smart way with ADEMP
text:
Why simulate?



When formulas fail, simulate
Real data are messy (missingness, nonlinearity, clustering)
Assumptions break in practice
We need to test “what if” scenarios safely
Simulations reveal if methods are robust, unbiased, and reliable










We simulate to “rehearse” real-world messiness. It’s a safe sandbox to see if a method holds up with missing data, small samples, or nonlinearity—before we bet a study’s conclusions on it.

title: Design and report simulation studies the smart way with ADEMP
Design and report simulation studies the smart way with ADEMP
text:
A : Aims
The aims define what the simulation study seeks to learn about a method’s statistical properties.
. . .






The Aim sets the compass. Are we stress-testing methods under realistic conditions, or just showing proof of concept? Clear aims avoid a common mistake: running simulations first and deciding later what they were for.

title: Design and report simulation studies the smart way with ADEMP
text:
A : Aims






Notice how the aims on the right are specific and testable. They ask focused statements about method performance under defined conditions. Good aims aren’t just “compare Method A and B”; they specify what aspect matters (bias? power? coverage?) and under what realistic scenarios. This specificity guides every downstream decision in the ADEMP workflow.

title: Design and report simulation studies the smart way with ADEMP
text:
D : Data-generating Mechanisms

The DGM is your virtual factory. It takes in certain parameters of interest as components and builds them into the outcome you wish to simulate
It’s where you decide what world your methods will live in — how realistic, how messy, how extreme they are. The more thoughtful your DGM, the more meaningful your conclusions.
If I want to test survival models, my DGM might simulate event times from a log-logistic distribution with right-censoring. I can vary the sample size or censoring rate to see how the method performs across contexts.
Parametric DGMs give you control and flexibility—you can systematically vary sample sizes, effect sizes, and distributions to stress-test methods across many scenarios. Resampling from real data keeps you grounded in reality but limits generalizability to that one observed dataset. In practice, many simulation studies use parametric DGMs informed by pilot data or literature estimates to balance realism and breadth.

. . .





. . .

Choose realism over simplicity
Parametric (known model) or resampling (real data)
Vary key factors (sample size, effect size, noise level)

. . .






Note



In planning a simulation study, it is usual to spend more time deciding on data-generating mechanisms than any other element of ADEMP.

title: Design and report simulation studies the smart way with ADEMP
text:
E: Estimands

The estimand is the target—the true parameter you care about. The estimator is the tool you use to hit that target. This distinction matters enormously in simulations because we know the true estimand by design, so we can directly measure how well each estimator performs. Confusing these leads to unfair comparisons, like testing whether a regression coefficient and an odds ratio are “the same”—they’re answering different questions.










The majority of simulations compare on specific quantities like means, \(\beta\) coefficients, odds ratios. Occasionally some other quantities are compared such as covariate adjusted vs unadjusted effects.


The goal is often to get estimates as close to the true value as possible (low bias).
\[\begin{equation*}
\text{Bias} = \mathbb{E}\left(\hat{\theta}\right) - \theta
\end{equation*}\]


Sometimes the estimand is actually more of a target like measures of predictive accuracy, sample size



. . .






Remember



Estimand ≠ Estimator
The estimand is what you want to estimate (\(\theta\)); the estimator is how you estimate it (\(\hat{\theta}\)).

title: Design and report simulation studies the smart way with ADEMP
text:
M : Methods







Define and justify each method
Ensure comparability (same estimand)
Report convergence issues, assumptions



The Methods are your competitors in a boxing ring. Just as in boxing where opponents are matched by weight and skill, methods ensure everyone estimates the same target.
If your methods are designed for different estimands, the comparison is unfair — like judging a fish and a bird on who climbs a tree faster.

text:
P: Performance
What we report



Measure
Meaning




Bias
Accuracy (closeness to truth)


SE / MSE
Precision / total deviation


Coverage
Interval reliability


Type I / Power
Test validity


MCSE
Simulation uncertainty



. . .






Remember!



Even simulations have uncertainty — that’s what MCSE quantifies.



These five performance measures are some of the key tools for evaluating methods.
Bias tells us about systematic error, MSE combines bias and variance into overall accuracy, coverage checks if confidence intervals are honest, power and Type I error assess testing procedures, and MCSE reminds us that even our simulation results have sampling variability. Always report MCSE alongside your estimates—it’s the measure of how much your simulation results would change if you re-ran it with a different random seed.

Tip



Bias measures systematic error: the average difference between your estimator and the true value (\(\theta\)). Small absolute bias is better.

Formula method

Formula-based sample size calculations are fast and convenient, but they rest on large-sample approximations that can break down exactly when we need them most—in small samples or at extreme proportions. The dropout adjustment here is just a crude inflation factor; it doesn’t model dropout as an actual stochastic process. Most importantly, the formula assumes a particular test statistic and doesn’t let us explore alternatives like exact tests or different handling of missing data. Simulation removes these limitations.

A — Aims

This table shows ADEMP in action. Notice how each element connects: the Aim defines what we’re looking for (minimum sample size for 80% power), the DGM specifies realistic data generation including dropout as a binomial process, the Estimand and Methods are aligned (both target the risk difference using prop.test), and Performance measures directly address the Aim. This upfront planning prevents scope creep and ensures every simulation run serves a clear purpose.

text:
Simulation function

#Parameters
n_enrolled <- 60
p0 <- 0.30
p1 <- 0.45
dropout <- 0.1
alpha <- 0.05

simulate_one_trial <- function(n_enrolled, p0, p1, dropout, alpha) {
  # Apply dropout to get observed sample sizes
  n0_obs <- rbinom(1, n_enrolled, 1 - dropout)
  n1_obs <- rbinom(1, n_enrolled, 1 - dropout)

  # Skip if either group is empty
  if (n0_obs == 0 || n1_obs == 0) return(NA)

  # Generate outcomes
  y0 <- rbinom(1, n0_obs, p0)
  y1 <- rbinom(1, n1_obs, p1)

  # Test for difference in proportions
  test <- prop.test(x = c(y1, y0), n = c(n1_obs, n0_obs))

  # Return TRUE if we reject H0
  test$p.value < alpha
}

# Run simulation for a given sample size
simulate_power <- function(n_enrolled, p0, p1, dropout,
                          nsim = 2000, alpha) {
  # Simulate nsim trials
  results <- map_lgl(1:nsim, ~ simulate_one_trial(n_enrolled, p0, p1, dropout, alpha))

  # Calculate power and MCSE
  power_hat <- mean(results, na.rm = TRUE)
  mcse <- sqrt(power_hat * (1 - power_hat) / sum(!is.na(results)))

  tibble(power = power_hat, mcse = mcse)
}

section: CI coverage: Wald vs Wilson (one proportion)
text:
CI coverage: Wald vs Wilson (one proportion)



set.seed(20251017)
nsim  <- 2000   # number of repetitions
n     <- 25     # sample size
p     <- 0.05   # true proportion
alpha <- 0.05   # nominal level

wald_cover   <- logical(nsim)
wilson_cover <- logical(nsim)

for (i in seq_len(nsim)) {
  x <- rbinom(1, n, p)      # data
  phat <- x / n

  # Wald (normal approx) CI
  z  <- qnorm(1 - alpha/2)
  se <- sqrt(phat * (1 - phat) / n)
  wald <- c(phat - z * se, phat + z * se)

  # Wilson (score) CI (no continuity correction)
  pr <- prop.test(x, n, correct = FALSE, conf.level = 1 - alpha)
  wilson <- pr$conf.int

  # Does each CI contain the truth?
  wald_cover[i]   <- (wald[1]   <= p && p <= wald[2])
  wilson_cover[i] <- (wilson[1] <= p && p <= wilson[2])
}

# Empirical coverage by method
coverage <- data.frame(
  method = c("Wald", "Wilson (score)"),
  cover  = c(mean(wald_cover), mean(wilson_cover))
)



















Conclusion



In small samples with low prevalence of the outcome, the Wald CI can undercover (<95%), while the Wilson (score) CI is typically much closer to nominal.



This example illustrates a classic problem with normal approximation methods: they fail when sample sizes are small or proportions are extreme. The Wald interval severely undercovers because its variance estimate becomes unstable with low event counts. The Wilson (score) interval inverts the test statistic and performs much better. Simulations like this reveal when textbook methods break down and guide us toward more robust alternatives for real applications.

text:
Pitfalls to Avoid

These pitfalls are unfortunately common in the published literature. Selective scenario reporting makes methods look better than they are. Seed shopping is a form of p-hacking for simulations—running multiple seeds and reporting the best one. Unfair tuning means extensively optimizing your new method while leaving competitors at default settings. Hidden failures occur when non-converged or errored runs are silently dropped rather than reported. And skipping MCSEs leaves readers unable to judge whether differences between methods are real or just simulation noise.

. . .
Don’t Do This


Selective scenarios: Cherry-pick favorable cases
Seed shopping: Try seeds until results look good
Unfair tuning: Optimize one method only
Hidden failures: Ignore non-convergence
No MCSEs: Report point estimates only

Pitfalls to Avoid

The antidotes to these pitfalls are straightforward: transparency and fairness. Pre-specify your scenarios before running simulations—treat it like a study protocol. Fix your random seeds and document them so others can reproduce your exact results. Give all methods equal tuning effort. Report convergence failures and sensitivity to them. And always include Monte Carlo standard errors so readers can distinguish signal from noise. Following these practices makes your simulation study credible and reproducible.



Don’t Do This

No MCSEs: Report point estimates only


Do This Instead


Pre-specify: Register scenarios upfront
Fix seeds: Document and share all seeds
Equal treatment: Same tuning for all
Report everything: Include failure rates
Always MCSEs: Quantify simulation uncertainty

text:
Takeaways

Let me leave you with this: ADEMP isn’t just an acronym—it’s a philosophy for rigorous simulation research. Each element plays a distinct role, and they must work together. Start with clear aims, design data generation that reflects reality, specify your target estimand explicitly, choose methods that actually estimate that target, and measure performance in ways that answer your aims. If you follow this structure and avoid the common pitfalls, your simulation studies will be transparent, reproducible, and genuinely informative for biostatistical practice.




Aims define purpose — keep them focused.
Data mechanisms define realism — make them plausible.
Estimands define truth — make them explicit.
Methods define action — justify every choice.
Performance defines evidence — quantify uncertainty.
